0.title: He Is There and He Is Not Silent
0.essay:
Imagine a God who made the world and then said nothing. You could look at the stars and know that someone great had been there. You could feel the weight of your conscience and know that someone holy was watching. But you would never know his name, or what he thought of you, or whether a guilty person could ever be welcome in his presence. The Bible begins somewhere else: “And God said” (Genesis 1:3).

A God who speaks

Francis Schaeffer gave one of his books the title He Is There and He Is Not Silent. That is the heart of this study. The living God has spoken: in the world he made, in the history of Israel, through prophets and apostles, and finally and fully in his Son. And he has caused what he said to be written down, so that people who never stood at Sinai or walked in Galilee can hear him too.

This study asks what that written word is: breathed out by God, true, authoritative, clear, sufficient and necessary. And at every step we will find that the Bible keeps pointing away from itself, to Christ.

What this study does not repeat

Several studies sit close by. How We Got Our Bible tells how the books were gathered, copied and translated. Hermeneutics teaches how to interpret them. The chapter “The Authority of Scripture” in The Doctrines of Grace sets out the Reformation principle of Scripture alone. Biblical Counseling and Knowing God’s Will apply Scripture to the care of souls and to our decisions. This study goes underneath them all, to the doctrine itself.

Why it matters

If God has spoken, the most important thing about any day is whether we listened. The doctrine of Scripture is really a doctrine about God: that he stoops to talk to his creatures, and keeps his word.

The chapters

God Has Spoken: Creation and Scripture; Breathed Out by God: Inspiration; True in All It Affirms: Inerrancy; The Voice of the King: Authority; Clear Enough to Obey: Clarity; Enough: Sufficiency; Necessary: Why We Cannot Live Without It; and The Word That Leads to the Word: Scripture and Christ.

For reflection

If you are honest, do you open your Bible expecting God to speak, or expecting to read about him? What do you think would change if you believed, every time you read it, that the living God was addressing you?

1.title: God Has Spoken: Creation and Scripture
1.essay:
Every human being lives under a sermon. It is preached each morning from the sky, in a language that needs no translation. Yet there is one thing this sermon never says, and it is the one thing a guilty person most needs to hear.

The sky is talking

David looked up and heard it: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the sky above proclaims his handiwork. Day to day pours out speech, and night to night reveals knowledge” (Psalm 19:1–2). Then a paradox: “There is no speech, nor are there words, whose voice is not heard. Their voice goes out through all the earth” (Psalm 19:3–4). The stars use no words, so every land understands them. A farmer in the Andes and a child in Glasgow hear the same message.

Paul says the same about every human being: “For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has shown it to them. For his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived, ever since the creation of the world, in the things that have been made. So they are without excuse” (Romans 1:19–20). God also speaks inside us. Even those without the Bible “show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness” (Romans 2:15). And he speaks through his daily kindness: “he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness” (Acts 14:17).

Theologians call this general revelation, because it is given to everyone, everywhere. The studies Common Grace and Faith & Science explore it further.

Why the sky cannot save

Surely, many say, a sincere person can find God in nature? Scripture answers no, for two reasons.

The first is what creation says. It tells us that God is mighty, wise and good; conscience adds that he is holy and we have broken his law. But nothing in a sunrise tells a guilty person how a holy God can forgive. The stars can announce a Judge. They cannot announce a pardon. That is news, and news must be told.

The second is how we hear. Paul says that people “by their unrighteousness suppress the truth” (Romans 1:18), and that “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but they became futile in their thinking” (Romans 1:21). The light is not too dim; our eyes are shut. So, as Positions at a Glance puts it, creation leaves people without excuse, not with a way of salvation. “The world did not know God through wisdom” (1 Corinthians 1:21). Someone has to tell it.

Two halves of one psalm

Psalm 19 itself shows the difference. In its first half, about the sky, God is called by the general Hebrew word for God. Then, without warning, the psalm turns: “The law of the LORD is perfect, reviving the soul; the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7). From here to the end, God is called “the LORD”, his covenant name, seven times. The sky tells you that God is glorious. Only his word tells you his name.

Notice too how the psalm moves. The sun goes round the heavens, “and there is nothing hidden from its heat” (Psalm 19:6). Then the word goes into the heart, and David cries, “Who can discern his errors? Declare me innocent from hidden faults” (Psalm 19:12). The sun searches the earth; the word searches the soul. And the psalm ends where creation could never take it: “O LORD, my rock and my redeemer” (Psalm 19:14). No star ever taught anyone to say my redeemer. C. S. Lewis thought this the greatest poem in the Psalter. It holds both of God’s books in one song.

Spectacles for weak eyes

John Calvin compared Scripture to spectacles. An old man with failing sight sees that a book is open but cannot read it; give him spectacles and the blur becomes words. So Scripture gathers up our confused knowledge of God and shows us the true God clearly. A Christian does not see less in a sunset than others do, but more.

Many times, many ways, and then a Son

God did not leave us with the sky alone. He gave what theologians call special revelation: words and deeds that tell what nature cannot. He called Abraham. He rescued Israel from Egypt and then explained through Moses what the rescue meant. He sent prophets. “Long ago, at many times and in many ways, God spoke to our fathers by the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son, whom he appointed the heir of all things, through whom also he created the world” (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Read that last phrase slowly. The Son through whom God spoke is the one “through whom also he created the world”. The one who made the speaking sky came and spoke in a human voice, on a hillside, in a boat, at a graveside. The Word that set the stars preaching without words came and preached in words. And God had his speaking written down, as the Westminster Confession says, for “the better preserving and propagating of the truth”.

An example

A nurse on night shifts used to stand in the hospital car park at dawn, watching the sky turn gold. She was sure someone had made it, and the thought made her uneasy, because of things in her life she could not undo. A colleague gave her Luke’s Gospel. When she reached the thief on the cross, she sat in her car and read it twice. The sunrise had told her that God was there. Only the book told her he was merciful.

For reflection

Why can creation and conscience bring a person to guilt but not to pardon? How does it change your reading of Psalm 19 to notice the move from “God” to “the LORD”? What does it mean to you that the Son who made the world is the one through whom God has now spoken?

2.title: Breathed Out by God: Inspiration
2.essay:
“By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 33:6). When Paul wanted to tell Timothy what the Bible is, he reached for the same picture. Scripture, he said, is breathed out by God. The breath that lit the stars stands behind the page.

Breathed out, not breathed into

“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (2 Timothy 3:16). How We Got Our Bible explains Paul’s Greek word. Here we notice three things.

First, inspiration describes the text. Paul does not say that the writers felt inspired, or that readers will find it inspiring, though both may be true. He says that Scripture itself, the written thing, came out from God. Second, it describes all of it: the genealogies and the Gospels, the laws and the laments. Third, Paul is speaking of the very writings Timothy had known “from childhood”, the Old Testament his mother and grandmother taught him, “which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15). Inspiration is not a scholars’ theory. It is a family Bible on a kitchen table, with God’s breath in it.

Down to the words

The New Testament shows that God’s breath reached the words, and not only the ideas. Jesus argued for the resurrection from three words: God told Moses, long after Abraham died, “I am the God of Abraham”, not that he had been, and so “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Paul built an argument on a singular noun: “It does not say, ‘And to offsprings,’ referring to many, but referring to one, ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ” (Galatians 3:16). This is why Positions at a Glance says that Scripture is God-breathed in its very words.

Men spoke from God

Peter tells us how it happened: “no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). Both halves matter. Men spoke: real people, with their own voices. From God: what they spoke had its origin in him. The early church prayed to the God “who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit” (Acts 4:25). One mouth, two speakers.

Many ways, one result

Hebrews says God spoke “in many ways”, and Scripture shows us some of them. Sometimes the words came almost as dictation. Jeremiah spoke and Baruch “wrote on a scroll at the dictation of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD that he had spoken to him” (Jeremiah 36:4). When the king burned that scroll, God simply had it written again (Jeremiah 36:32). Kings can burn paper. They cannot unsay God.

But most of Scripture did not come like that. Luke did research. He talked to eyewitnesses and wrote, “it seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you” (Luke 1:3). John wrote from memory, helped by the promise that the Spirit would “bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you” (John 14:26). Paul answered news: “it has been reported to me by Chloe’s people” (1 Corinthians 1:11). He used a secretary, who slipped in his own greeting: “I Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord” (Romans 16:22). The psalmists wrote out of tears and joy.

You can hear the differences. Mark hurries from scene to scene. John uses a small vocabulary with endless depth. Paul’s great opening to Ephesians runs on as one long sentence in Greek, as if he cannot stop. God did not flatten these voices. As Positions at a Glance puts it, the Spirit guided the writers through their own personalities, not by mechanical dictation.

God prepared the writers

How can a book be fully human and fully God’s? Part of the answer is that God prepared the people long before they picked up a pen. He told Jeremiah, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). Paul spoke of God “who had set me apart before I was born” (Galatians 1:15). Each writer’s temperament, schooling and sorrows were shaped by God’s providence. B. B. Warfield made the point well: if God wanted to give his people letters like Paul’s, he prepared a Paul to write them. So we never have to choose between “Paul wrote Romans” and “God wrote Romans”. Both are wholly true.

Jesus’ Bible

Above all, we take our view of Scripture from Jesus. “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished” (Matthew 5:17–18). The iota was the smallest letter; the dot, a tiny stroke of the pen. Jesus held that even these stood firm.

He quoted the narrator of Genesis as the voice of the Creator: “he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, and said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother’” (Matthew 19:4–5). He said that David spoke “in the Holy Spirit” (Mark 12:36). Facing his enemies, he rested on a single word of a psalm, and added, “Scripture cannot be broken” (John 10:35). And on the night of his arrest, when he could have called on legions of angels, he refused: “But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?” (Matthew 26:54). He went to the cross because the Bible said he would. If Jesus is Lord, he is Lord of how we read it.

An example

A retired engineer had always assumed that “inspired” meant the writers went into a trance. Reading Luke 1:1–4 in a church study group, he stopped. “He checked his sources,” he said. “He wrote a report.” For the first time he saw that God had used a careful man’s care. Far from weakening his trust, it made the Bible feel like a real book from a real God.

For reflection

Which of the “many ways” God used surprises you most? How does it help to know that God prepared each writer before he wrote? What does Jesus’ own use of Scripture ask of you?

3.title: True in All It Affirms: Inerrancy
3.essay:
A promise is only as good as the person who makes it. One of the strangest preachers in the Old Testament, a prophet hired to curse Israel, found himself saying instead: “God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind. Has he said, and will he not do it?” (Numbers 23:19). If God breathed out Scripture, its truth rests on his.

Your word is truth

On the night before he died, Jesus prayed for his disciples: “Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth” (John 17:17). He did not say merely that God’s word is true, as a report might be true. It is truth: the measure of everything else. “Every word of God proves true; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him” (Proverbs 30:5). “The words of the LORD are pure words, like silver refined in a furnace on the ground, purified seven times” (Psalm 12:6).

Scripture is breathed out by God, and God is the one “who never lies” (Titus 1:2); indeed “it is impossible for God to lie” (Hebrews 6:18). So this commentary holds, in the words of Positions at a Glance, that Scripture as first given is without error in all it affirms. This is inerrancy.

What inerrancy does not claim

The words “in all it affirms” matter. Truth is judged by what a writer means to say, by the standards of his time and his kind of writing. The Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978) made the same point. Inerrancy is not spoiled by things like these.

Round numbers. Numbers says that those who died in the plague at Peor “were twenty-four thousand” (Numbers 25:9). Paul, recalling the event, says “twenty-three thousand fell in a single day” (1 Corinthians 10:8). Paul may count one day only, or both may be round figures; neither offers a census.

Everyday description. “The sun rises, and the sun goes down” (Ecclesiastes 1:5). Weather forecasters still say that. Jesus called the mustard seed “the smallest of all seeds” (Matthew 13:32): the smallest a Galilean farmer sowed. He was speaking of his hearers’ fields, not writing botany. Faith & Science says more.

Paraphrase in quotation. Ancient writers had no quotation marks and often gave the sense of what was said. At Jesus’ baptism, Matthew reports the Father’s voice as “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17), and Mark as “You are my beloved Son” (Mark 1:11). The meaning is identical.

Different angles. The charge nailed above the cross appears four ways: “This is Jesus, the King of the Jews” (Matthew 27:37); “The King of the Jews” (Mark 15:26); “This is the King of the Jews” (Luke 23:38); “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews” (John 19:19). John adds that it was written in three languages (John 19:20). Each gives the part that served his account; four honest witnesses rarely use the same words.

Accurate reports of false words. Scripture faithfully records the serpent saying, “You will not surely die” (Genesis 3:4). It is true that he said it; it is not true that it was so. The Bible affirms what it teaches, not everything it reports.

Two hard places, honestly

Some passages are genuinely difficult. Here are two.

First, the blind men at Jericho. Matthew says that “as they went out of Jericho … there were two blind men sitting by the roadside” (Matthew 20:29–30). Mark names one, Bartimaeus, “as he was leaving Jericho” (Mark 10:46). Luke has one blind man “As he drew near to Jericho” (Luke 18:35). Mentioning one does not deny that there were two; Mark gives the name of the one the church later knew, and Luke tells his story too. As for leaving and approaching, Jericho in Jesus’ day had two sites, the ancient town and Herod’s newer one nearby, so the healing may have happened between them. Others think Luke’s phrase can simply mean “while he was near Jericho”. We cannot be sure which is right. But this is just the kind of difference independent witnesses produce. Had the writers agreed a story, it would have been smoothed away.

Second, Solomon’s horses. One verse says “Solomon also had 40,000 stalls of horses for his chariots” (1 Kings 4:26); the parallel says “Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots” (2 Chronicles 9:25). Four thousand fits his “1,400 chariots” (1 Kings 10:26). Most likely a scribe miscopied the number in Kings. As Positions at a Glance says, such differences in numbers between Samuel, Kings and Chronicles are copying slips, not errors in Scripture as first given; How We Got Our Bible tells how the copies let us find them.

Humility and patience

Augustine once wrote to Jerome that when he met something in Scripture that seemed contrary to the truth, he would conclude that the copy was faulty, or the translator had missed the sense, or that he himself had not understood. That is not dishonesty, but the patience we give any witness who has proved reliable. Many confident claims of error have since been cleared up. Belshazzar was long unknown outside Daniel, until Babylonian texts showed him ruling for his absent father, which explains why he could make Daniel only “the third ruler in the kingdom” (Daniel 5:29). We can hold a question open without holding God at arm’s length.

Where Christians differ

Some sincere Christians, including fine scholars, hold that the Bible is infallible in what it teaches about salvation and godliness, but may contain incidental mistakes of history or science. They want to be honest with the hard places and not make faith so brittle that one puzzle can topple it. That concern deserves respect.

This commentary’s view: Scripture is without error in all it affirms, because Jesus himself drew no line between the “religious” and the “historical” parts of his Bible; he spoke of Noah and of Jonah as real history (Matthew 24:37–39; Matthew 12:40). The faith is woven into history: “if Christ has not been raised, then our preaching is in vain and your faith is in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:14). And Jesus asked, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3:12). A book that can be trusted with what we can check can be trusted with what we cannot: forgiveness, the resurrection and the life to come.

An example

A young man watched an online video listing a hundred “contradictions” in the Bible and felt his faith slipping. He and his pastor chose six from the list and worked through them over coffee. Five dissolved on a careful reading. The sixth they left open. “I don’t need to solve every puzzle today,” he said at the end, “to know who I can trust.”

For reflection

Which of the things inerrancy does not claim was most helpful to you? How might Augustine’s patience change the way you handle a hard passage? Which promise of God are you most glad you can trust completely?

4.title: The Voice of the King: Authority
4.essay:
“Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool,” says the LORD. No temple could hold him. Then comes a surprise: “But this is the one to whom I will look: he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word” (Isaiah 66:1–2). The King of all things is looking for people who tremble at what he says.

Authority follows authorship

If God breathed out Scripture, then when Scripture speaks, God speaks. The Westminster Confession says that its authority does not depend on any person or church, but wholly on God, who is truth itself and its author. We do not lend the Bible authority by agreeing with it.

The crowds felt this in Jesus: “he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew 7:29). Paul thanked God that the Thessalonians had received his preaching “not as the word of men but as what it really is, the word of God, which is at work in you believers” (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

What does trembling look like? When young King Josiah heard the rediscovered Book of the Law, “he tore his clothes” (2 Kings 22:11), and God said, “because your heart was penitent … I also have heard you” (2 Kings 22:19). Trembling is not the cringing of a slave, but the humility of someone addressed by the one who matters most, who finds that the God who speaks also listens.

Over tradition

Jesus loved the Scriptures and was hard on traditions that smothered them. Some religious leaders allowed a man to declare his money “given to God” and so escape caring for his elderly parents. Jesus called this “making void the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down” (Mark 7:13).

This is what the Reformers meant by Scripture alone. Parents, elders, governments and the historic creeds all have real authority, but Scripture alone is the final and unerring one. As Positions at a Glance puts it, councils deserve respect where they agree with Scripture, as Nicaea and Chalcedon do, but they can err, and no church may bind the conscience beyond God’s word.

Other Christians see it differently, and deserve to be heard at their best. Roman Catholic teaching, as the Second Vatican Council set it out, presents Scripture and Tradition as flowing from the same divine source, with the church’s teaching office as their authentic interpreter; it adds that this teaching office is not above the word of God but serves it. Orthodox Christians speak of Scripture as the heart of Holy Tradition, read within the church’s living memory. Both are right that the Bible was never meant to be read by individuals cut off from the church’s long wisdom.

The question is what happens when the church and the Bible disagree. The Bereans tested even an apostle, “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so” (Acts 17:11), and Luke calls them noble for it. Paul put himself under the same rule: “even if we or an angel from heaven should preach to you a gospel contrary to the one we preached to you, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:8). The church is “a pillar and buttress of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15): it holds the truth up, as a lampstand holds a lamp. It does not light it.

Over experience

Our age is more tempted to set experience over Scripture than tradition. Peter had seen Jesus transfigured and heard the Father’s voice on the mountain. Yet he writes, “we have the prophetic word more fully confirmed, to which you will do well to pay attention as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Peter 1:19). Peter, who heard God speak from heaven, points his readers to the written word.

In Jesus’ parable, when the rich man begs that someone be sent back from the dead to warn his brothers, Abraham replies, “If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be convinced if someone should rise from the dead” (Luke 16:31). Experiences can be real and precious, but Scripture is their test.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that if we keep only the parts of the Bible we already agree with, we are left with a God who can never contradict us, and a God who can never contradict us is hard to tell apart from our own reflection. A real person sometimes says what we do not want to hear. So does a real God.

How we come to be sure

How does anyone become sure that the Bible is God’s word? The Westminster Confession answers wisely. The church’s testimony can move us to respect the Bible, and the Bible itself offers many evidences: the heavenliness of its subject, the power of its teaching, the majesty of its style, the agreement of all its parts, its aim of giving all glory to God, and the way it makes known the only way of salvation. Yet, the Confession says, “our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth, and divine authority thereof, is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit, bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts.”

Notice the words “by and with the Word”. The Spirit does not whisper extra information alongside the Bible. He opens our eyes to see what is already there, as a man’s eyes recognise light. Jesus said, “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:27). A sheep does not prove its shepherd’s voice by argument. It knows it. Christians call Scripture self-authenticating: like the sun, it is seen by its own light.

An example

A man in his forties felt a strong sense of peace about leaving his wife for a woman at work. God wanted him to be happy, he told a friend. The friend did not argue with his feelings. He opened Malachi 2 and Matthew 19 and asked him to read them aloud. There was a long silence. “I knew,” the man finally said. “I just didn’t want it to be God saying it.” It was the beginning of his coming home.

For reflection

What would it look like for you to “tremble” at God’s word this week? Where are you most tempted to let tradition, church culture or experience overrule Scripture? Why is it important that the Spirit bears witness “by and with the Word”, not apart from it? Has the Bible ever contradicted you? What happened?

5.title: Clear Enough to Obey: Clarity
5.essay:
Moses stood with Israel on the edge of the promised land and told them something remarkable about God’s word: “this commandment that I command you today is not too hard for you, neither is it far off. It is not in heaven … Neither is it beyond the sea … But the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it” (Deuteronomy 30:11–14).

Near, not far

Many religions keep the truth at the top of a mountain, for the spiritual athletes who can climb there. Moses says the opposite: God has put his word near.

Paul picks up these very words and applies them to the gospel. No one needs to ask, “Who will ascend into heaven?” (Romans 10:6), for “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Romans 10:8), and that word, he explains, is “the word of faith that we proclaim” (Romans 10:8). Christ has come down, and the message about him is close enough to believe. The clarity of Scripture is part of the good news: God has made the way to himself plain.

Light for the simple

“Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). “The unfolding of your words gives light; it imparts understanding to the simple” (Psalm 119:130). Psalm 19 says the same: “the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple” (Psalm 19:7). In the Old Testament the “simple” are not the stupid, but the inexperienced and easily led: the young, the untaught, people like most of us. God’s word is made for them.

God expected ordinary families to understand it. Parents were to teach his words to their children and “talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way” (Deuteronomy 6:7). Jesus held people responsible for what they had read, again and again asking, “Have you not read …?” (Matthew 12:3). Paul’s letters were read aloud to whole congregations, and he addressed the children directly: “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1). He expected them to understand.

Honest about hard things

Clarity does not mean every verse is easy. Peter said of Paul’s letters, “There are some things in them that are hard to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16). It is comforting that even an apostle found Paul hard going at times.

The Westminster Confession states the doctrine carefully: “All things in Scripture are not alike plain in themselves, nor alike clear unto all”. Yet the things we must know, believe and do to be saved are so plainly set out somewhere in Scripture “that not only the learned, but the unlearned, in a due use of the ordinary means, may attain unto a sufficient understanding of them.” Some passages may puzzle us all our lives. The way of salvation is not among them.

Notice where Peter puts the blame for twisting: not on the text, but on “the ignorant and unstable”. Often the deepest difficulty is not in the lamp but in our eyes. “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him” (1 Corinthians 2:14). So the risen Jesus did something no commentary can do: “he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45). Every reader can pray, “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18).

Teachers and the church

Clarity does not make teachers unnecessary. The Ethiopian official reading Isaiah was asked if he understood, and answered honestly, “How can I, unless someone guides me?” (Acts 8:31). Christ gives “the shepherds and teachers, to equip the saints” (Ephesians 4:11–12). Good teachers are a gift. But see what Philip did: “beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35). A good teacher makes the text plain and then steps back, so that you see it for yourself.

Roman Catholic teaching holds that Scripture needs the church’s teaching office to give its authentic meaning. Its concern is real: individuals do misread the Bible, and Protestants have divided too easily. But an infallible interpreter would himself need interpreting, and the cure for bad reading is better reading, together, under the Word. William Tyndale, who translated the New Testament and much of the Old into English from the Greek and Hebrew, and was put to death in 1536, is reported to have told a learned opponent that he would make a boy who drives the plough know more of the Scriptures than he did. The Reformers believed the Bible was made for ordinary people.

The ordinary reader with the Bible in hand

So read it. Read whole books, not only single verses. Let the plain passages light the hard ones, and never build a doctrine on one obscure verse. Read with your church, and test what you hear by what is written. Hermeneutics gives more help.

Gregory the Great, a bishop of Rome around AD 600, compared Scripture to a river in which a lamb can wade and an elephant can swim. It is shallow enough for a child at the edge and deep enough to drown the proudest scholar. The infinite God stooped to speak so plainly that a child can understand him, and so deeply that eternity will not exhaust him.

An example

A man who left school at fourteen and worked all his life on a farm was given a Bible by his daughter. He started with Mark, one chapter a night at the kitchen table. In chapter 2 Jesus says to a paralysed man, “Son, your sins are forgiven” (Mark 2:5). He read it several times and then called his daughter. “It means me, doesn’t it?” he said. It did.

For reflection

Have you ever assumed the Bible was too hard for you, and why? How do Deuteronomy 30 and Romans 10 connect the clarity of Scripture with the gospel? How can you make use of teachers without leaning on them in place of reading for yourself? Which book of the Bible could you read through this month?

6.title: Enough: Sufficiency
6.essay:
We live in an age of add-ons. Phones need apps, diets need supplements, and many Christians quietly treat the Bible the same way: good as far as it goes, but in need of an upgrade. The doctrine of sufficiency says that for the purpose God gave it, nothing is missing.

Complete, equipped

Paul tells Timothy why Scripture was breathed out: “that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:17). Not some good works: every one.

Peter says the same with even wider arms: “His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us to his own glory and excellence” (2 Peter 1:3). Notice where the sufficiency lies: “through the knowledge of him”. Scripture is enough because it gives us God himself, made known in Christ. A Bible that needed supplementing would imply a Christ who needed supplementing. But “in him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily, and you have been filled in him” (Colossians 2:9–10).

What sufficiency says

The Westminster Confession puts it this way: the whole counsel of God about everything necessary for his own glory and for our salvation, faith and life is “either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture”, and nothing is ever to be added, “whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men.”

Moses drew the line that keeps us sane: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children forever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deuteronomy 29:29). There are two halves to that verse, and both are mercies. God has not told us everything: why this illness, why this delay, when the end will come. Those secret things are his, and we can leave them with him. But what he has told us is ours, and it is enough to live by today.

The freedom of enough

Sufficiency is a doctrine of freedom. If Scripture is enough, then no church, preacher or inner voice may lay on your conscience a rule God has not given. Paul was indignant with teachers who added their own: “‘Do not handle, Do not taste, Do not touch’ … according to human precepts and teachings” (Colossians 2:21–22). Such rules, he says, look wise but “are of no value in stopping the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). And Proverbs warns, “Do not add to his words, lest he rebuke you and you be found a liar” (Proverbs 30:6).

For the anxious and over-scrupulous this is good news. There is no secret extra requirement you have missed. God has said what he requires, and in Christ he has supplied it.

What sufficiency does not mean

The doctrine is easily misused. Scripture is sufficient for what it was given for: to make us “wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15) and to equip us for a godly life. It is not a textbook of medicine, engineering or accounting. It will not tell you how to set a broken arm or design a bridge. God gives that knowledge through his world, by the ordinary gifts of study, skill and research, which are themselves his kindness.

So using doctors and medicine is no failure of faith. One of the Gospel writers was “Luke the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Paul, an apostle through whom God worked miracles, told Timothy: “use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). When God promised King Hezekiah fifteen more years, Isaiah still said, “Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover” (Isaiah 38:21). God’s promise and a poultice of figs were not rivals.

Nor does sufficiency mean the Bible tells you which job to take or whom to marry. It gives you wisdom, boundaries and a Father who cares, and then gives you freedom to choose. The study Knowing God’s Will explores this.

Sufficient for the soul

This is why this commentary holds both things together in the care of souls. God’s word is sufficient for life and godliness. Our deepest problem is always spiritual, and no therapy can forgive sin or give a new heart. Yet the body matters too, and much suffering, including much depression, is suffering, not sin.

So for an ongoing struggle, such as anxiety, depression, an addiction or the effects of past abuse, go first to a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up. Medical treatment, including medication where a doctor advises it, is no failure of faith. And in an emergency, if you are thinking of ending your life or someone is in danger, get help the same day: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or tell someone you trust now. The study Biblical Counseling says much more.

An example

A woman in a long season of low mood was prescribed an antidepressant, and left it in the cupboard for weeks. She feared that taking it would mean she did not trust God. Her biblical counsellor met with her each week. They read Psalm 42 and Psalm 88 together, and the counsellor encouraged her to follow her doctor’s advice. “The pills are not your hope,” she said. “Christ is. But he may use the pills, the way he uses sleep and food.” Over months, slowly, both her mood and her prayers began to lift.

For reflection

Where are you tempted to feel that the Bible is not quite enough? How does Deuteronomy 29:29 help you with questions God has not answered? Why is it important to say both that Scripture is sufficient and that medicine is no failure of faith?

7.title: Necessary: Why We Cannot Live Without It
7.essay:
After forty days without food in the wilderness, Jesus was hungry, and the devil suggested bread. Jesus answered with a sentence from Deuteronomy: “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God’” (Matthew 4:4). He did not only quote it. He lived it, starving, at the moment it cost most.

Bread for the soul

Moses first spoke those words about the manna. God “humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna … that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but man lives by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD” (Deuteronomy 8:3). Israel was hungry in order to learn what they were really hungry for.

The Bible speaks of itself as food, not dessert. “Like newborn infants, long for the pure spiritual milk, that by it you may grow up into salvation” (1 Peter 2:2). “Your words were found, and I ate them, and your words became to me a joy and the delight of my heart” (Jeremiah 15:16). And Psalm 119, the longest chapter in the Bible, is one long love song to God’s word from someone who knew he could not survive without it: “If your law had not been my delight, I would have perished in my affliction” (Psalm 119:92). Scripture was not decoration on his life. It was the difference between perishing and living.

No faith without hearing

Scripture is also necessary for salvation itself. Paul traces a chain: “How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:14–15). Then he draws the conclusion: “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17).

We saw in the first chapter that creation can tell people there is a God, but cannot tell them of Christ. That is why the word is necessary. The Westminster Confession says that God committed his revelation wholly to writing, and that this makes Scripture “most necessary”, since his former ways of revealing his will have now ceased. It is why Christians send missionaries and translate the Bible into new languages, as Missions & the Nations describes.

The sword that leads to the priest

“For the word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and of spirit, of joints and of marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Hebrews 4:12). We need the Bible because it reads us. It finds the motives we hide even from ourselves. “And no creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him to whom we must give account” (Hebrews 4:13).

That would be terrifying if the passage stopped there. It does not. In the very next breath: “Since then we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus, the Son of God … Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:14–16). The word cuts like a surgeon, not an assassin. It lays us open so that it can lead us to the priest who was “in every respect … tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).

Why not a new word beside it?

Should we also expect fresh words from God today? This commentary’s position is set out in Positions at a Glance: God’s speaking in his Son is final; the Spirit now illumines and applies Scripture and gives no new revelation beside it, so claimed voices, impressions and dreams must be tested by the completed word. The faith has been “once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 3).

Many Christians we respect see this differently. Continuationists such as Wayne Grudem and D. A. Carson hold that the gift of prophecy continues today in a fallible form that must always be tested by Scripture. They do not claim such words equal the Bible, and they agree that it is the final judge. We gladly own them as brothers. But we hold that a word claiming to come newly from God would in effect add to Scripture, and we notice a quiet danger: in practice the fresh voice tends to get more attention than the old book.

Isaiah faced a people tempted to seek guidance elsewhere, from mediums who would consult the dead. His answer still stands: “To the teaching and to the testimony! If they will not speak according to this word, it is because they have no dawn” (Isaiah 8:20).

And we do not lose the living voice of God by holding to Scripture. Hebrews introduces a psalm with the words “as the Holy Spirit says, ‘Today, if you hear his voice’” (Hebrews 3:7). Not “said”. Says. When the Bible is read, the Spirit is speaking now, in the present tense, to you. The study Knowing God’s Will applies this to our decisions.

The famine

Amos warned of a terrible judgment: “I will send a famine on the land, not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD” (Amos 8:11). In Samuel’s boyhood “the word of the LORD was rare in those days” (1 Samuel 3:1). A famine of the word can come even to a house with four Bibles on the shelf, if none is opened. It is possible to starve in a bakery.

An example

A father of three young children noticed that he had not opened his Bible for months. He was simply busy. But he was more irritable, more anxious, and quicker to fill quiet moments with his phone. He started again with one chapter of John each morning before the house woke up. Some mornings little seemed to happen. Within a few weeks his wife asked him what had changed.

For reflection

When have you felt the difference between being fed by God’s word and going without it? How does Hebrews 4:12–16 change the way you think about being searched by Scripture? Are you looking for a word from God beside the one he has given?

8.title: The Word That Leads to the Word: Scripture and Christ
8.essay:
On the first Easter evening two disciples walked home to Emmaus, heartbroken. A stranger joined them. It was the risen Jesus, but they did not know him. And before he let them see who he was, he gave them a Bible study: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

The Bible study on the road

Why not simply show them his hands? Perhaps because he was about to leave their sight, and wanted their faith anchored where it could survive his absence: in what was written. We will not walk that road with him either. But we have what they were given that evening. Afterwards they said, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?” (Luke 24:32).

Later that night he did the same for the others: “everything written about me in the Law of Moses and the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled” (Luke 24:44). Those were the three parts of the Hebrew Bible. All of it, he said, is about him. “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:46–47). The cross, the empty tomb and the gospel going to the world: this is what the whole Old Testament was reaching for. Even the prophets were moved by “the Spirit of Christ in them” as he “predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories” (1 Peter 1:11). The studies Christ in the Old Testament and Reading the Old Testament Well trace this in detail.

Searching without coming

Jesus said to the most devoted Bible students of his day, “You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life” (John 5:39–40).

It is possible to know the Bible well and miss the point. The Scriptures are a signpost, and a signpost is honoured not by being admired but by being followed. Everything we have said in this study, that Scripture is breathed out, true, authoritative, clear, sufficient and necessary, is for this: that we might come to Christ and have life. A high view of the Bible that does not lead to Christ is not high enough.

An example

A woman had read her Bible every day for twenty years, mostly out of duty. It felt like homework. Then a friend suggested she read Luke 24 and, from then on, ask one question of every passage: what does this show me of Jesus? She began in Genesis. By Exodus she was reading late into the night. “I had been reading a rulebook,” she said. “Now I’m reading about someone I love.”

The Word made flesh

John begins his Gospel with words that gather up the whole of this study: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Then: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

God’s speech has a face. The one who said “Let there be light” became a baby who could not yet speak. “No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known” (John 1:18). The Greek word for “made him known” is the root of our word exegesis, the careful explaining of a text. Jesus is the explanation of God. The written word tells us of him; he is the Word it tells of.

There is a likeness here, not an identity. Christ is fully God and fully man, without sin. Scripture is fully God’s word and fully human words, without error. We worship Christ, not the book. But we love the book because it carries him to us, as Mary’s arms carried the child.

Every promise, yes

So the whole Bible holds together in him. “For all the promises of God find their Yes in him” (2 Corinthians 1:20). That is why the word cannot fail: “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever” (Isaiah 40:8). Peter quotes those words and then tells us what that everlasting word is: “And this word is the good news that was preached to you” (1 Peter 1:25).

And at the very end, when John sees heaven opened and a rider on a white horse coming to judge and make war, he tells us the rider’s name: “the name by which he is called is The Word of God” (Revelation 19:13). The title of this study is, in the end, a name. The Word of God is a person, and he is coming back.

Until the day dawns

Peter called Scripture “a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Peter 1:19). A lamp is for the night. One day we will not need it. Of the city to come, John says, “They will see his face … They will need no light of lamp or sun, for the Lord God will be their light” (Revelation 22:4–5).

Until then, the lamp is precious beyond words, because it is lit from his face. When many turned away from Jesus, he asked the Twelve if they would go too. Peter answered for every believer who has ever loved this book: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). We love the Bible not because we love paper and ink, but because on every page the one who loved us and gave himself for us is speaking. Open it, and ask him to do again what he did on the Emmaus road. He still makes hearts burn.

For reflection

Why do you think the risen Jesus opened the Scriptures to the two disciples before he let them recognise him? What does it mean to you that the rider in Revelation 19 is called “The Word of God”? What could you do this week to read your Bible looking for him?
